A1-A2.headline: Why the UK Stopped Killing Badgers

pages.text:
For years, the UK tried killing wild badgers to stop a bad illness in farm cows. That illness gave farmers big trouble.

The old plan has now stopped, with no active passes left as of May 2026.
pages.caption: A European badger in its natural home.

pages.text:
Wild badgers in Europe are safe under a 1992 UK law. Because of this rule, the plan caused loud public talks.

Teams needed special legal papers before they could take part in the work on farms.
pages.caption: The entrance to a badger home.

evidence.articleCaption: The entrance to a badger sett down which gas canisters are thrown during gassing

pages.text:
Science tests gave mixed answers over the years. Experts watched what happened after badgers left a farm area.

The badgers that stayed began to walk much farther than before. Their family groups changed, and some animals brought the illness into new fields where healthy cows lived.

The whole plan cost 58.8 million pounds by 2024. Many people asked if the high price was worth the mixed results.

Now that the old plan is over, the UK government is using health shots instead. Leaders hope this kind step will keep farm cows safe while caring better for wild animals.

B1-B2.headline: Changing Strategies for Bovine Tuberculosis in the UK

pages.text:
For years, the UK used badger culling to fight bovine tuberculosis, a germ illness hitting farm cattle. It stayed a tough problem for farmers.

The policy has now ended, with no active licenses as of May 2026.
pages.caption: A European badger in the wild.

pages.text:
European badgers are legally protected under the Protection of Badgers Act 1992. That status made the control policy strongly debated across the country.

Teams needed special state licenses to carry out the plan.
pages.caption: The entrance to a badger sett.

evidence.articleCaption: The entrance to a badger sett down which gas canisters are thrown during gassing

pages.text:
Long field trials showed mixed and uncertain outcomes. Experts saw a clear movement trend called the perturbation effect when local badger numbers fell.

Surviving animals ranged farther across nearby land, broke up group bonds, and sometimes spread the illness into fresh cattle herds.

Total public spending on the policy reached 58.8 million pounds by 2024, raising sharp questions across the country about its true value.

Now that the culling plan has ended, the UK government is using vaccine programs to manage the disease while supporting stronger care for animal welfare.

Causing a lot of public disagreement.

C1-C2.headline: The Evolution of UK Bovine Tuberculosis Control Policies

pages.text:
For decades, UK authorities deployed badger culling to curb bovine tuberculosis, a pervasive bacterial contagion afflicting livestock.

That contentious intervention concluded entirely, leaving zero active licenses by May 2026.
pages.caption: A European badger in its habitat.

pages.text:
Because European badgers enjoy statutory safeguards under the Protection of Badgers Act 1992, lethal management provoked sustained public scrutiny.

Implementation consequently demanded extraordinary legal licensing exceptions.
pages.caption: A badger sett entrance.

evidence.articleCaption: The entrance to a badger sett down which gas canisters are thrown during gassing

pages.text:
Empirical field trials yielded ambiguous epidemiological conclusions, complicating policy justification. Ecologists documented a pronounced perturbation effect following localized population reductions.

Displaced survivors expanded their territorial foraging ranges, destabilizing social structures and inadvertently disseminating pathogens across adjacent farmland.

Cumulative public expenditure escalated to 58.8 million pounds by 2024, prompting rigorous reassessment of cost-effectiveness.

Following the programme's formal termination, UK policymakers now prioritize immunological vaccination protocols, balancing agricultural biosecurity alongside heightened wildlife welfare obligations.
